prompt: Explain how the U.S. Supreme Court works using only bass-fishing tournament metaphors. Keep going well past the point where it makes sense.
response:
The United States Supreme Court is not a court of law; it is the ultimate Elite Series Championship weigh-in, held on the treacherous, unmarked waters of Constitutional Lake. The nine Justices are not jurists, but elite anglers who have fished the circuit for decades, earning their spot on the boat through a grueling nomination qualifier and a Senate confirmation cull that checks their tackle box for ideological lures.

When a case is granted certiorari, it is akin to a tournament director announcing that a specific, legendary stump in the backwaters is now in play. The lower courts are merely the local B.A.S.S. Nation opens; they catch fish, sure, but their weights don’t count toward the all-time record book. Only when the Supreme Court launches its aluminum hull at dawn does the true pattern emerge.

Oral arguments are the morning bite window. The attorneys are not advocates; they are co-anglers sitting in the front seat, desperately trying to convince the Justice-angler that their specific plastic worm is the only thing triggering strikes in this current. If an attorney’s presentation is weak, it’s like backlashing your baitcaster on the first cast; the Justice will immediately reel you in, snip your line, and retie with a knot of skepticism. A sharp questioning from the bench is not judicial inquiry; it is a violent hookset on a submerged log, testing whether the legal theory has the tensile strength to withstand the drag setting of originalism or the elasticity of living constitutionalism.

The conference room where the Justices meet in private is the livewell. Here, the catch is sorted. Some fish are culled immediately because they lack the minimum length of standing or were caught out of season due to mootness. The remaining fish—the viable precedents—are measured against the golden ruler of *stare decisis*. But beware: a fish that measured 24 inches in 1973 might suddenly shrink to 18 inches when placed on the modern scale of textualism, forcing the anglers to throw back a catch that generations of fishermen swore was a trophy.

Opinion drafting is the art of selecting the right lure color for murky water. The majority opinion is the primary pattern, the chartreuse-and-white spinnerbait that everyone agrees is producing.
